name: Automating Trade Settlement
title: Automating Trade Settlement
answer: Automating trade settlement covers the post-trade steps that move a trade from execution to final exchange of cash and securities, including trade matching, confirmation, reconciliation, settlement instruction generation, and exception handling. It sits within agent workflows in finance, where software agents perform operational tasks that were previously handled by back-office staff. The scope includes equities, fixed income, foreign exchange, derivatives, and repo across custodians, clearinghouses, and internal systems. The aim is to reduce manual touchpoints and shorten the time between execution and settlement, often supporting T+0 or T+1 cycles where regulation permits. It does not include pre-trade decision-making or execution algorithms.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Automating trade settlement covers the post-trade steps that move a trade from execution to final exchange of cash and securities, including trade matching, confirmation, reconciliation, settlement instruction generation, and exception handling. It sits within agent workflows in finance, where software agents perform operational tasks that were previously handled by back-office staff. The scope includes equities, fixed income, foreign exchange, derivatives, and repo across custodians, clearinghouses, and internal systems. The aim is to reduce manual touchpoints and shorten the time between execution and settlement, often supporting T+0 or T+1 cycles where regulation permits. It does not include pre-trade decision-making or execution algorithms.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These agents run on existing post-trade infrastructure such as central securities depositories, custodial networks, SWIFT messaging, and internal reconciliation systems. They typically operate as a software layer that reads from trade capture systems, order management systems, and market utility feeds. Compute is usually cloud or on-premise servers with secure access to financial messaging APIs. Many deployments combine large language models for reading unstructured settlement instructions and exception notes with deterministic rules engines for matching and payment routing. Data storage must meet the audit and retention requirements of the relevant market regulator.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by breaking settlement into a pipeline of agent tasks: trade capture validation, enrichment of standing settlement instructions, matching against counterparty confirmations, cash and position reconciliation, and exception handling. Agents use rule-based logic for deterministic steps and machine learning for classifying unmatched items or free-text messages. A human-in-the-loop review is common for exceptions that exceed confidence thresholds or involve failed trades. The agent may draft settlement messages, propose corrective actions, and log every decision for audit. Work is orchestrated by a workflow engine that tracks state and deadlines.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance centers on auditability, error liability, and regulatory compliance. Every action an agent takes must be traceable to the input data, model version, and rule set that produced it. Risk includes incorrect settlement instructions, missed deadlines, and unauthorized changes to payment details, so access controls and dual control remain important. Provenance records should show which agent or human approved each step, especially for exception resolutions. Financial regulators may require that firms retain the ability to explain and reconstruct settlement decisions, and that final responsibility remains with a licensed or accountable person.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward fully straight-through processing with agents handling most routine settlement tasks and escalating only genuinely ambiguous cases. As market infrastructures move to shorter settlement cycles, agents will need to operate in near real time across time zones and multiple currencies. Future systems may coordinate multiple agents across firms, using standardized message formats and shared ledgers to reduce reconciliation. The role of human staff will shift from data entry and matching to oversight, exception design, and control testing. Adoption will depend on regulatory acceptance of agent decisions and on the reliability of provenance and audit trails.
